title: 'It is not panic stations': Why the second season was always going to test Mark Milligan's Jets

 SAVE $60 All articles from our website & app The digital version of Today's Paper All other regional websites in your area Continue That's the question Newcastle fans are asking after a giant-killing run under Mark Milligan last season has so far failed to transfer into the new campaign.
 The Jets are winless across three different competitions, are still without a chief executive after Tain Drinkwater's shock resignation in June and face another enormous task at home on Tuesday night.
 Jets striker Nikos Vergos has a shot saved against Wellington. Top right, Joe Lolley muscles past a a defender. Bottom right, James Delianov shows his disappointment. Picture by Darren Pateman, AAP Three days after going down to Wellington 3-0 in the A-League, the Jets take on Chinese juggernaut Shanghai Port FC in the Asian Champions League Elite at McDonald Jones Stadium.
 A fourth loss in a row would all but end their hopes of progressing to the knockout stage of the mega-rich tournament.
 While the fortunes may appear clouded, players-turned-experts Daniel McBreen and Roy O'Donovan have urged the Jets faithful to be patient.
 "It is not panic stations yet," said McBreen, who will call the ACLE match for broadcaster Paramount Plus. 
 "The second year is always harder when you do well in the first year as a player and as a coach.
 "The Jets took everyone by surprise last year. This season, opposition coaches expect them to play that brand of football. They are all ready for it.
 "Plus you have to replace the players who have left. You can't deny that they lost five starters - Eli Adams, Lachie Rose, Clayton Taylor, Mark Natta and Lachie Bayliss. 
 "The goals they lost are a big one for me.
 "I think it is going to take a little bit of time.
 "Do we see the signs of the football the Jets played last year? Yes.
 "Do I think Mark Milligan is a one-hit wonder? Not at all.
 "I think Millsy is a good coach and I think he will be a great coach. This is a difficult year for him."
 O'Donovan, who played 77 games for the Jets, believes his former club has the coach and the players to revive their season.
 "I don't fear for them," said the striker-turned-pundit for Paramount Plus.
 "In my mind, they are going to finish in the top four this season."
 The Jets, after winning the Australia Cup last year, made a slow start to the league season, losing four of opening five games.
 The issues then were in defence. They scored nine goals, but leaked 14.
 "Last season, five games in and we were thinking was the Australian Cup a fluke," McBreen said.
 "Then they hit their straps and off they went."
 O'Donovan was critical of the new-look attack, which has netted three goals in the ACLE and three in the A-League, but remains confident that the tide will turn.
 "My concern is that they are not taking their chances," O'Donovan said.
 "In the second half against Wellington, and the week before in the first half against Macarthur, they were so dominant with the ball.
 "Nikos Vergos's all-round game is terrific. He is a really good target, he runs the channels and holds the ball up really well.
 "As a striker he need to score, he needs to get off the mark in the A-League and I think he will be a different player.
 "They have signed Joe Lolley. Zac Clough is looking fit and is a very good player. Alex Badolato is a back from an ACL injury.
 "With the likes of Clough, Max Burges and Will Dobson, they will open up defences for fun.
 "The earlier in the game they are clinical and take those chances, the more the Jets will run away with it.
 "But it will take a little time for it to click into gear."
 Time is not a luxury the Jets have in the ACLE.
 Shanghai Port have won consecutive Chinese Super League titles, are coached by Kevin Muscat, have an annual budget of about $130 million and have been in Australia since Thursday preparing for the round four clash.
 The Jets are lining up for their fourth game in 10 days and are seemingly running on empty.
 "As great as it was to win the premiership last year, which came with the added bonus of getting the Jets into the Asian competition, they don't have the budget nor the squad at the moment to balance both competitions," O'Donovan said. "You can see that."
 The venture into Asia has resulted in lopsided losses to Kashima (7-1) Gamba Osaka (3-1) and Kyoto Sanga (5-2).
 "Playing in the ACL Elite is extremely difficult," McBreen said. "For Australian teams to be competing on that stage with lesser budgets and younger players, that is really, really difficult.
 "And it does have a knock-on affect. 
 "Mark Milligan wants to keep playing the way his team wants to play, but they keep getting stung in the tail.
 "In the last game, Kyoto brought on two Brazilians and went bang, bang, bang.
 "It happened in the game before as well. "
 Milligan said on Monday that he wants his young squad to "continue to be brave" and play "our football".
 "It is still very early in the journey of this group. There are no red flags to say we are not on the right path," Milligan said.
 Muscat said in his pre-game news conference on Monday that he hadn't kept close tabs on the A-League but noted a "drastic difference in squads" at the Jets.
 "A lot of players have left and maybe the squad is not as young as it was," Muscat said. "In the early stages with a younger squad, they played some good football. They were entertaining and from a distance seemed to be doing very well."
